name: Bulwarden
author: jgloeckl.de

sections.description:
Bulwarden is the site agent, installed on each managed WordPress site. It
exposes a signed REST API (jgm/v1) that a Bulwarden hub calls to read
health and security data, run checks and trigger updates. The hub is a separate
application — it is not part of this plugin — and this plugin talks to no hub
at all until you pair it with one. On its own it sends nothing anywhere.

It is built for the person who is responsible for a site they did not build:
an agency looking after forty of them, or an owner who wants one place that
answers “is this thing all right?” without logging into it.

What it reports

  • Site health — WordPress, PHP and plugin versions, pending updates, disk
    usage, and WordPress’ own Site Health tests, collected in one snapshot.
  • A full plugin and theme inventory, with each item’s version, whether it
    is active, whether an update is waiting, and whether it came from
    WordPress.org at all — which is what lets a hub match it against a CVE feed.
  • Must-use plugins, which WordPress runs on every single request with
    nothing activating them and no way to switch one off from the admin. Nothing
    else in wp-admin lists them properly, and dropping a file there is the tidiest
    way to install a backdoor.
  • Configuration-level security checks with a posture score — file editing,
    directory listing, XML-RPC, debug output, and the rest of the settings that
    quietly decide how exposed a site is.
  • Unfinished updates. An update that already replaced a site’s files can
    still fail to finish, and neither state clears itself: a pending database
    schema upgrade that every administrator is sent to and the public site hides
    completely, or a leftover .maintenance lock from an updater that died
    mid-copy. Both are reported, and both can be finished from the hub by running
    exactly what WordPress itself would have run.
  • Email delivery. WordPress keeps no record of the mail a site sends: when
    a contact form stops delivering or an order confirmation never arrives, the
    error is raised and thrown away. This counts what was attempted, what failed
    and why, and reports which transport is doing it — PHP’s mail(), an SMTP
    server, or the plugin that configured one. No part of any message is stored:
    not the recipient, not the subject, not the body.

What it finds

  • A malware scan in three layers. Every core and WordPress.org file is
    verified against its published checksums, so a modified file is found
    whether or not anybody has written a signature for what was put in it; then
    every file is read for the code patterns webshells and injected backdoors
    actually use. Findings carry the file, the line and a short excerpt.
  • Backdoors that arrive dressed as an ordinary plugin — a forged
    administrator login, a privileged action gated on a key baked into the file,
    an account created from hard-coded credentials, users hidden from the users
    list. A plugin absent from WordPress.org has no published files to check it
    against, so without this a hostile one surfaced only as unverifiable.
  • A plugin hiding itself. Malware that conceals a plugin does it by
    answering the question before WordPress can — and the hidden plugin is then
    also the one plugin whose files are never checked. The scan counts what is on
    disk itself and compares.
  • Server-configuration files. .htaccess, php.ini and .user.ini are
    the one part of a WordPress install that changes what the server does
    rather than what WordPress does, and nothing in wp-admin shows them. A file
    set to run before every request, a rule that makes uploaded images execute as
    PHP, a redirect that only fires for search engines: all reported, with the
    line. Nothing is ever changed for you — a good share of those directives are
    written deliberately by a host or a security plugin, and the point is that
    you get to decide which.
  • Leftover files. An interrupted backup, a finished restore and a migration
    plugin all leave things behind and none of them clean up: a
    wp-config.php.bak the web server hands out as plain text, a database.sql
    in the web root, an installer that overwrites the site with no login. Found,
    measured, and removable from the hub — and the site decides what may be
    deleted, so a stale list can only ever be refused.
  • Signatures that keep up. The scan’s pattern list comes from your
    provider rather than from this plugin, so a new detection reaches the site in
    hours rather than waiting for a release to travel a whole fleet. The plugin
    itself contains no malware signatures at all — a file full of them is exactly
    what a hosting provider’s own malware scanner flags — and the site keeps the
    list it receives in its database.
  • A scan that starts itself. When a plugin WordPress.org does not publish
    appears in the plugins or must-use folder, the site starts a scan within
    seconds and tells your provider what set it off, instead of waiting for the
    next scheduled one. Fake plugins are how most WordPress break-ins arrive, and
    a scan is a cheap thing to be wrong about: nothing is blocked, quarantined or
    deleted — the site looks, and your provider decides.

What it does

  • Remote core, plugin and theme updates, wrapped in maintenance mode so
    visitors never see a half-updated site — and taken off the host’s PHP time
    limit, so a core update on shared hosting finishes instead of being killed
    part-way.
  • Zero-knowledge encrypted backups. The archive is built and encrypted on
    this server    , under a passphrase that is never transmitted anywhere;
    only the ciphertext is uploaded. Nobody — including whoever runs the hub —
    can read a backup without that passphrase.
  • Restores that fail safely. The same thing in reverse, and it can put back
    the database alone if that is all that broke. Every table is rebuilt beside
    the live one and swapped in only once it is complete, so a restore stopped by
    a timeout or a server limit leaves the database exactly as it was rather than
    half-replaced — and picks itself back up where it stopped. What could not be
    done is counted and reported rather than discarded, so a restore that ran into
    trouble says so instead of reporting success.
  • Page tracing. Your provider can ask this site to render one of its own
    public pages and report which file produced each line of the HTML — core, a
    plugin, the theme, a must-use plugin. It answers the question nothing in
    WordPress answers: which plugin adds the Google Fonts tag, or the tracking
    script, or the markup nobody can find a setting for. The page is never
    altered to do it.
  • WP-Cron on a schedule that actually runs. A site with no visitors runs no
    cron, which is how scheduled posts, order emails and licence checks quietly
    stop.
  • A support card on the dashboard naming whoever maintains the site, how to
    reach them, and a Request help button that files a ticket with them
    directly — attached to the right site, without the owner having to explain
    which one.
  • An activity log on the site itself, append-only, recording everything that
    changed this site or sent part of it somewhere — and which side asked. Updates
    installed by your provider and anything that failed with them, backups,
    restores, scans, repairs, deleted leftovers, a file read off the server, a
    traced page, and every change to the credentials, the passphrase or the
    provider details. WordPress records what changed and never who asked, and the
    answer belongs on your own server rather than only in somebody else’s console.

Pairing

On activation the plugin provisions an API key + secret. Copy the connect
string from the Bulwarden entry in the WordPress admin menu and paste
it into the hub’s “Connect a site” form. Your provider’s support details are
then pushed to the site automatically by the hub and appear on the dashboard.

No hub account yet? Until the site is paired, the plugin’s banner and settings
screen offer Start a free trial, which opens the Bulwarden hub’s pricing
page (https://hub.bulwarden.net/pricing/) in a new tab. Start a trial there,
set your password from the email you receive, choose “Connect a site” in the
hub and paste the connect string. Opening that page sends nothing from this
site; it is an ordinary link.

Security

Hub → client requests are authenticated with the per-site API key and an
HMAC-SHA256 signature over the method, route, timestamp, a single-use nonce and
the body. The nonce is what makes a signature good exactly once: it is recorded
when the request arrives and refused if it comes back, so a captured request
cannot be replayed. Timestamps outside a 5-minute window are rejected outright,
which is also how long a nonce has to be remembered for. The secret never
travels on the wire — it lives only in this plugin and in the hub webapp.

Privacy

Bulwarden is a client agent: on its own it sends data nowhere. Pairing this
site with a hub (yours, or your maintenance provider’s) is an explicit,
opt-in action — you choose when to copy the connect string from the Bulwarden
screen in the WordPress admin menu and hand it to that hub. Nothing is
transmitted before that.

Once paired, data only moves in these cases:

  • Health, inventory, and security checks. The paired hub reads these from
    this site’s signed REST API when it polls or when a check is requested —
    WordPress/plugin/theme versions and update status, a full plugin & theme
    inventory, disk usage, and the configuration-level security posture score.
  • Backups, only when triggered (the Settings screen’s “Back up now”
    button, or a request from the paired hub): the full site is archived and
    encrypted on this server with a passphrase that is never transmitted
    anywhere, then the ciphertext is uploaded to the hub. Only someone who has
    the passphrase can decrypt a backup — the hub operator cannot read its
    contents.
  • Malware scan results, only when a scan is triggered (admin- or
    hub-initiated): findings (type, severity, file path, line, and a short
    excerpt) are sent to the hub that requested the scan.
  • Finishing an interrupted update, when the paired hub asks. Nothing is
    sent in that exchange; the site runs WordPress’ own database upgrade, or
    deletes an expired .maintenance lock file, and reports the outcome.
  • Server-configuration files, when the paired hub asks: the contents of
    this site’s .htaccess, php.ini and .user.ini files, so the hub can show
    what is in them and when they last changed. These are configuration, not
    content — no post, page, media file or user data is read.
  • Email counters, as part of the health snapshot: how many messages this
    site attempted and how many failed over the last seven days, the error text
    the mail server returned, and which transport is sending. No part of any
    message is recorded     — not the recipient, not the subject, not the body.
  • A traced page, only when the hub asks for one: the HTML of a single
    public page of this site, exactly as an anonymous visitor would receive it,
    plus the file paths and line numbers that produced it. No file contents are
    read and no logged-in view is ever rendered.

Independently of any hub pairing, this plugin verifies WordPress core and
wordpress.org-hosted plugin files by comparing local file hashes against the
public checksum APIs at api.wordpress.org and downloads.wordpress.org.
Those requests carry only what identifies the release to look up — the
WordPress version and locale, and each plugin’s slug and version. No file
contents, hashes, URLs or user data are sent: the reference checksums come
back and the comparison happens here, on this server.

Bulwarden does not call home on activation, does not collect analytics, and
stores data on no server this site hasn’t been explicitly connected to. The
hub itself is a separate service outside this plugin’s control; consult your
provider for how it handles the data described above.

External services

This plugin connects to the services below. Nothing here runs on activation.

Your Bulwarden hub

Bulwarden is the site-side agent for a hub — the management application an
agency or site owner runs to watch and maintain a fleet of WordPress sites. The
hub is a separate product and is not part of this plugin.

The default hosted hub is operated by Bulwarden at https://bulwarden.net/ —
terms of use: https://bulwarden.net/terms/ , privacy policy:
https://bulwarden.net/privacy/ . A hub can also be self-hosted, or run by the
maintenance provider you buy from, in which case this plugin talks to that
provider’s server instead and their terms and privacy policy apply.

No connection to any hub exists until you make one. You pair a site by
copying the connect string from the Bulwarden screen in the WordPress admin
menu and pasting it into the hub; before that the plugin contacts no hub at
all, and it never discovers or chooses one on its own. Once paired, data moves only in these cases:

  • When the hub asks for status. It reads this site’s signed REST API and
    receives WordPress/plugin/theme versions and update status, the full plugin
    and theme inventory, disk usage, the results of WordPress’ own Site Health
    tests, and the configuration-level security posture score.
  • When a backup runs (you press “Back up now”, or the hub requests one).
    The site is archived and encrypted here, with a passphrase that is never
    transmitted, and only the ciphertext is uploaded. The hub operator cannot
    read a backup’s contents without that passphrase.
  • When a malware scan runs (started by you or by the hub). The findings —
    type, severity, file path, line number and a short excerpt — are sent to the
    hub that asked for the scan.
  • When the hub pushes your provider’s support details — their name, logo,
    support address and accent colour — on connect and whenever they change
    them. Nothing is sent from the site in that exchange.

Every one of those requests is authenticated with this site’s own API key and
an HMAC-SHA256 signature; the shared secret never travels over the wire.

api.wordpress.org and downloads.wordpress.org

The malware scan verifies WordPress core and wordpress.org-hosted plugins
against their published checksums, using WordPress.org’s own public APIs at
https://api.wordpress.org/core/checksums/1.0/ and
https://downloads.wordpress.org/plugin-checksums/. This happens whenever a
scan runs, whether or not the site is paired with a hub.

These requests identify only the release being looked up: the WordPress version
and locale, and each installed plugin’s slug and version. No file contents,
hashes, site URL or user data are sent — the reference checksums are returned
and compared locally.

These are WordPress.org services, covered by the WordPress.org privacy policy:
https://wordpress.org/about/privacy/
sections.installation:
Bulwarden is one half of a pair: this plugin runs on the site, and a hub
runs somewhere else and manages it. Installing the plugin on its own does
nothing until you pair it with a hub.

  1. Install and activate the plugin as you would any other — upload it under
    Plugins → Add New → Upload Plugin, or install it from the directory.
  2. Go to Bulwarden in the WordPress admin menu. The plugin generated an
    API key and secret for this site on activation; the screen shows a single
    connect string that carries the site name, URL and both credentials.
  3. Copy that string and paste it into your hub’s “Connect a site” form. That is
    the whole pairing step — there is nothing to type on this side, and no
    hub address to configure here.
  4. If you want encrypted backups, set a backup passphrase on the same
    screen. It never leaves this server, and it is required to restore. Keep it
    somewhere you will still have it after the disaster you are backing up
    against — nobody, including your hub operator, can recover a backup
    without it.

Do I need a hub?

Yes, for anything beyond installing it. The hub is separate software: use the
hosted one, run your own, or use the one your maintenance provider runs. Until
the site is paired, this plugin contacts nothing and does nothing.

Upgrading

Updates install like any other plugin. Your credentials, passphrase and settings
survive an update; nothing needs re-pairing.
sections.faq:
Does this plugin send my site’s data anywhere on its own?

No. Before you pair it with a hub it contacts nothing at all, and it never
discovers or chooses a hub by itself. After pairing, data moves only for the
things listed under Privacy below — health checks, backups, malware scan
findings — and only to the hub you paired with.

Can the hub operator read my backups?

No, provided you set a passphrase. The archive is encrypted on this server
with a key derived from your passphrase, and only the ciphertext is uploaded.
The passphrase is never transmitted, so a hub holds bytes it cannot decrypt.
The same property is why nobody can recover a lost passphrase for you.

What happens if I deactivate or delete the plugin?

The site stops answering its hub, which the hub will notice and report as the
agent going unreachable. Deleting the plugin removes its settings, its audit-log
table and its working directories (see uninstall.php); backups already stored
on a hub are unaffected.

Is the plugin available in German?

Yes. Everything the plugin puts on screen — the settings page, the support
card on the dashboard, every status message and every scan finding — is
translated, and WordPress picks it up from your site’s own language setting with
nothing to configure. Both German locales are covered: Deutsch and Deutsch
(Sie). The wording is formal throughout, because these screens are read by the
owner of the site rather than by the agency that maintains it.

Does it work on multisite?

The plugin runs per site. A network-wide database upgrade is reported but not
performed — core’s own network upgrade screen walks every site in the
network, and that is where it belongs.

Network activation is not supported: it sets the plugin up for the main site
only, and every other site in the network would have no credentials to be
paired with. Activate it on each site you want managed, from that site’s own
Plugins screen, and pair each one with the hub separately.

Why does the malware scan flag a file I know is fine?

The file-integrity check compares every core and WordPress.org-hosted file
against the checksums WordPress.org published for that exact release. A caching
or optimisation plugin that rewrites a stylesheet produces the same mismatch a
backdoor does, which is why “this file no longer matches what was published” is
reported as a fact rather than a verdict, and why non-executable files are
warnings rather than critical findings. Your hub can show you the actual diff.

What does it do to my site’s performance?

Nothing on page loads: there is no front-end code path. Backups and malware
scans are real work and run in the background across WordPress cron ticks, to a
time budget, so they do not block visitors. Health checks are answered on demand
when the hub asks.

Which PHP and WordPress versions are supported?

PHP 7.4 or newer and WordPress 6.0 or newer. Backups additionally need the
sodium extension (encryption) and either zlib or the zip extension
(archiving); the Settings screen tells you if either is missing.
sections.changelog:
1.43.1

  • Fixed: the malware signatures your provider sends are now stored on the site in an encoded form, so a hosting provider’s malware scanner reading the database, or a database backup made by another plugin or by the host, no longer mistakes them for malware. Signatures already stored are converted the first time the updated plugin loads.

1.43.0

  • Maintenance: every release is now checked with VirusTotal before it is published; no change to how the plugin behaves.

1.42.0

  • Fixed: some hosting providers’ malware scanners flagged the plugin’s own scanner files as malware and suspended the site. The plugin no longer contains any malware signatures: your maintenance provider sends them to the site, which stores them in its database rather than in a file.
  • Changed: the “Scan signatures” tile on the plugin screen now says when the site has not yet received the signatures from your provider. Until then a malware scan still checks the site’s files against the official WordPress versions, but cannot look for known attack code, and your provider is told so rather than shown a clean result.

1.41.1

  • Maintenance: release of 1.41.0’s improvements with an internal code-style fix; no change to how the plugin behaves.

1.41.0

  • Improved: the malware scan now finds the files of a web-shell kit seen on hacked WordPress sites in October 2026, which hides its commands by writing them as numbers, plants file uploaders, installs a hidden must-use plugin and replaces pages with gambling spam. Several of its files were missed before.
  • New: the scan now reports PHP code in the plugins or themes folder that belongs to no plugin or theme — for example in a hidden folder — because WordPress never runs such a file and it can only be reached directly by its address.
  • Improved: the scan now also reads files named like file.php.tmp or file.php.bak, which many servers still run as PHP, and looks for the kit’s background process files in the server’s temporary folders.

1.40.2

  • Maintenance: internal code-style fixes only, no change to how the plugin behaves.

1.40.1

  • Improved: the plugin lock now also covers must-use plugins. When a site is locked, a must-use plugin dropped in after the lock is moved out of the mu-plugins folder instead of being allowed to run.

1.40.0

  • New: your maintenance provider can set a site to “lock” plugins — no new plugins can be installed or activated at all. Existing plugins keep working and still receive updates, and you can still deactivate a plugin; only adding or switching on a new one is blocked. This is off unless your provider turns it on.

1.39.0

  • New: if a plugin that is not from the WordPress.org directory appears on your site and then crashes every page, Bulwarden now switches it off by itself and brings the site back, instead of leaving it down until someone notices. It only does this to a plugin that arrived in the last few days; the files are left in place so they can be examined.
  • New: your maintenance provider can set your sites to hold a new plugin that is not from the WordPress.org directory — switching it off the moment it appears and turning it back on only once a scan is clean, or only once the provider approves it. This is off unless your provider turns it on. A plugin you install yourself is held for a moment, not blocked.
  • Improved: the malware scan now recognises a plugin that creates a hidden account and gives it administrator powers while calling it an “editor”.

1.38.1

  • Improved: the malware scan now recognises a fake plugin that creates a hidden account with full administrator rights while calling it an “editor”, so it does not look like a new administrator. This is what the fake “maintenance toolkit” plugins installed on several sites in October 2026 do. Such a plugin is now reported as malware.

1.38.0

  • New: the malware scan now finds PHP code hidden in “.cache” files, and in any file that an .htaccess tells the server to run as PHP whatever its name. This is how the malware in the compromised Rank Math SEO PRO 3.0.123 update stays on a site, and until now the scan never opened those files. Such a file is reported as a warning, or as critical when the server is set up to run it or the code looks like an attack. Cache files that only store data are not reported.
  • New: the server-configuration check now reads .htaccess rules that span several lines, and says which kinds of file a rule makes the server run as PHP. A rule that makes data, cache or image files run as PHP is reported as critical.
  • New: the malware scan reports a folder in your site’s main directory that has the same name as one of your published pages (for example “about-us”) and contains an index file. The web server shows that folder instead of your real page, which is how some spam kits take over a page without touching WordPress. It is a warning, or critical when the folder shows search engines something different from visitors.

1.37.5

  • Improved: if you installed Bulwarden yourself from the plugin directory, the “not connected yet” banner, the setup steps on the Bulwarden screen and the dashboard card now offer a “Start a free trial” button. It opens the Bulwarden hub in a new tab, where you can start a trial and then connect this site with its connect string. Nothing is sent from your site when you click it. If a provider asked you to install the plugin, connect the site to them as before; the button disappears once the site is connected.

1.37.4

  • Fixed: on sites behind a page cache with few visitors, a malware scan could take a day or more to finish, because each step of the scan waited for somebody to visit the site before the next one started. The scan now starts its next step itself, so it finishes in minutes. Restores already worked this way and now share the same mechanism.
  • Improved: malware scans are much faster on sites with large media libraries. Images, videos, PDFs and other media files in the uploads folder are still checked for hidden PHP code, but the full set of malware signatures is only run on them when they actually contain PHP. On a test site with 9,000 images a scan went from five minutes to under two.

1.37.3

  • Fixed: on sites where another plugin or a code snippet restricts the WordPress REST API to logged-in users (for example the “Disable REST API” option in Admin and Site Enhancements), every request from the maintenance hub was refused before Bulwarden could check it, so the site could not be paired, monitored or backed up. Requests signed by the hub are now let through that restriction, for Bulwarden’s own routes only; the rest of the REST API stays restricted, and nobody is logged in.

1.37.2

  • Fixed: the malware scan was meant to look for PHP files in the cache folder (wp-content/cache) since 1.35.0, but on every site using the default backup settings it never did, because that folder is left out of backups by default. Leaving the cache out of backups no longer keeps the scan out of it. Only PHP files there are checked, so the scan does not slow down on a large page cache. If you want part of the cache left alone, exclude that subfolder instead.

1.37.1

  • Fixed: on sites with large media folders the malware scan could keep re-reading the same folder and never finish. A folder that needs more than one pass now continues where the previous pass stopped, so every file is read once.
  • Fixed: if the web host stopped the scan’s background process abruptly, the scan was left half-finished with nothing to resume it. The scan now arranges its next step before it starts working, so it picks up again by itself within ten minutes.

1.37.0

  • New: your maintenance provider can ask the plugin what it is doing right now — whether a backup, malware scan or restore is running, how far it has got, and whether the scheduled tasks it waits for are running on time. Nothing is started or changed by asking, and no passwords, keys or file contents are included in the answer.

1.36.1

  • Fixed: signing in with one click from your maintenance provider could end on the message “This sign-in link is not valid any more” even though the sign-in had worked — on sites where you were already signed in, and on sites using a custom login address. The link is still used exactly once; a browser that already holds an administrator session is now taken straight to the dashboard instead of being shown the error.

1.36.0

  • New: your maintenance provider can check more than the homepage after an automatic update. The plugin lists the site’s pages — shop pages such as the checkout and the cart are marked — so the provider can pick the ones that matter, and each is compared before and after the update.
  • New: for pages that only show their real content to a signed-in visitor, such as a customer account, the provider can ask the site to create a read-only account called bulwarden-check. It can do nothing but read, cannot sign in with a password, and is only ever signed in for a few minutes by the automatic check. If its role is ever given more rights, the site stops signing in as it. Deleting the account switches this off.
  • Every creation of that account and every check sign-in is recorded in the activity log.

1.35.0

  • New: the malware scan now checks the wp-content/cache folder for PHP files with code in them. Attackers who exploit a caching plugin write their web shells there, and the scan used to skip the folder entirely. Only PHP files are read, so a large page cache costs little; generated pages, stylesheets and images are never opened. Every PHP file found there is also checked against the full signature table.
  • Compiled Blade views (Sage/Acorn), compiled Twig templates (Timber) and generated data files are recognised and not reported.
  • A very large cache is reported as not fully checked, rather than treated as clean.

1.34.1

  • Maintenance release: code-style fixes only, with no change in behaviour.
    It carries everything listed under 1.34.0.

1.34.0

  • Security: a long backup can no longer undo settings changed while it
    ran.     Regenerating the connection credentials, setting a backup
    passphrase or a change of hub address during a backup used to be reverted
    when the backup finished.
  • Security: signed requests from your agency’s hub now refuse anything added
    to the address that the signature does not cover, and each request stays
    single-use for its whole validity window.
  • Security: the site keeps more secrets out of what it sends your agency.
    Scan excerpts from configuration copies, database dumps, exports and logs
    are redacted; password files and connection strings in server
    configuration are no longer sent; files that look like keys, dumps or
    backups are never handed out for a comparison; and a failed restore’s
    error messages no longer quote the data that failed.
  • Fix: restores now finish correctly on Windows hosting and other servers
    that store table names in lower case. Tables with capital letters in
    their name (Wordfence’s, for example) kept their old contents before.
  • Fix: the site shows its maintenance notice while a restore writes files
    back, not only while it writes the database.
  • Fix: a malware scan that takes longer than an hour is no longer restarted
    from the beginning every hour, and a new scan no longer runs alongside the
    one it replaced.
  • Fix: the leftover-file check no longer offers a running restore’s working
    folder for deletion.
  • Hardening: a restore’s working files now have unpredictable names, and the
    copy of this site’s connection details it keeps is removed as soon as it
    has been used.
  • Fix: a restore that runs out of disk space now stops and says so, instead
    of reporting half-written files as restored.
  • Fix: a restore that fails part-way no longer leaves a second copy of the
    database behind in temporary tables, and backups never include them or a
    restore’s working folder.
  • Fix: a malware scan that runs out of memory on the site, or cannot save its
    progress, is now reported as failed instead of never finishing.
  • Fix: restores protect this plugin’s own folder and working folders on sites
    with a customised folder layout, and a relative auto_prepend_file that
    works is no longer switched off after a restore.
  • Security: the site only sends backups and scan results to, and fetches
    restores from, the hub it is paired with; a restore rejects a backup file
    with impossible sizes before reading it; signed requests and one-click
    sign-in links can no longer be used twice by two requests arriving at the
    same moment; the health report no longer lists subscribers and shop
    customers; and deleting the plugin now also removes its working folders.
  • Multisite: network activation is not supported — activate the plugin on
    each site you want managed.

1.33.1

  • Security: malware scan excerpts sent to your agency no longer include
    passwords in a few more cases     the earlier protection missed: settings
    stored as plain text, passwords written in capital letters, passwords
    containing an escaped quote, and logins inside web addresses. Posts
    behind a password, and form entries some plugins store as posts, are now
    treated as private.
  • Fix: an interrupted plugin update can no longer make a folder-specific
    scan rule run on every file.

1.33.0

  • New: the malware scan now reports program code added to a plugin’s or the
    active theme’s folder.     For every plugin published on WordPress.org, and for
    the active theme, the scan already checks that each file the release contains
    is unchanged; it now also reports a PHP file in that folder that the release
    does not contain at all, which is where an attacker hides a backdoor next to
    genuine files. Empty guard files and protected data files are not reported.

1.32.0

  • New: the malware scan now reports PHP files with code in the uploads
    folder.     Attacks through vulnerable file-upload features in plugins almost
    always leave a small PHP file there, and it stays behind after the plugin
    is updated. Harmless files that plugins put there on purpose, such as empty
    “Silence is golden” files, protected data files and known plugin files like
    Borlabs Cookie’s, are not reported.

1.31.1

  • Security: a password in wp-config.php or in a site setting is now always
    left out of scan findings, however short it is. Before, a password shorter
    than six characters could appear in a finding.
  • Fix: if an update of this plugin was interrupted halfway, leaving old and
    new files side by side, a malware scan could stop with an error. It now
    finishes with the plugin’s own detection rules until the update completes.

1.31.0

  • New: the malware scan now also checks the database. Many attacks never
    leave a file behind: they put a script into a post, hide code in a site
    setting, create an extra administrator or schedule a task that brings the
    attack back. The scan now looks at posts, settings, user accounts and
    scheduled tasks, and reports an administrator account that exists but is
    hidden from the Users screen.
  • New: your provider can now respond to a new attack within hours instead
    of waiting for a plugin update.     Besides the code patterns it already
    sends, it can now send the file names an attack drops, extra types of
    program file to report, patterns for the database checks above, and rules
    that apply only to certain folders or file types.
  • New: a scan now always uses your provider’s latest detection rules. Before,
    a site could run for up to six hours on the previous set.
  • Security: findings from wp-config.php and from the database never include
    passwords, keys or other secrets. The finding still shows what matched,
    with the secret replaced by its length.

1.30.1

  • Fix: one malware signature, the one that looks for preg_replace() with the
    long-removed /e modifier, could take far longer than it should on files
    containing long regular expressions, and on some files gave up without an
    answer. It now checks those files quickly and reliably, and still finds
    what it is meant to find.

1.30.0

  • New: the malware scan now recognises files that known attacks leave
    behind by their name.     Some exploits drop a marker or a web shell under a
    fixed name, and the name is often the only thing about the file that never
    changes. The first entries cover the WordPress file-inclusion attack
    (CVE-2026-87902) seen in September 2026.
  • New: the scan now also looks in the server’s temporary folders (/tmp,
    /var/tmp, /dev/shm), where that attack parks its payload before using
    it. Only files your own site created are looked at, so on shared hosting
    other customers’ files are never read or reported. A PHP file there that
    matches no known signature is reported as information only, because some
    template engines legitimately keep compiled files there.

1.29.3

  • Fix: a restore that could not write some files still reported a clean
    finish.     A folder the web server had lost write access to meant dozens or
    hundreds of files quietly not restored, under a green “Finished” badge. The
    files it deliberately leaves alone — your wp-config.php, the maintenance
    plugin itself, WordPress’ drop-ins — still count as a clean restore, as they
    should; the ones it tried and failed to write now say so.
  • Fix: “remove files the backup does not contain” now says which folder it
    could not clean out.     It deliberately never empties a folder your backup has
    nothing for — otherwise a backup taken without your plugins folder would
    delete every plugin on the site — but it only mentioned that in the run log.
    Since this is the option you would use to clear out a hack, and must-use
    plugins are where one usually hides, the restore now names the folder it
    skipped where you will see it.
  • Fix: a file that is a shortcut (symlink) is now listed when a backup skips
    it.     Backups never follow shortcuts, which is correct, and skipped folders
    were already listed; skipped files were not — so a site whose uploads or
    configuration files are linked in from elsewhere had them missing from the
    backup with nothing saying so.
  • Fix: a backup that failed to download during a restore reported the raw
    network error. It now says the backup could not be fetched and that nothing
    on the site was changed, with the technical detail after it.

1.29.2

  • Fix: a backup corrupted every percent sign in your site’s content and
    settings, and a restore put the corruption back.     Each % was written into
    the backup as a 66-character marker, so prices like “50% off”, CSS widths and
    percent-encoded links came back mangled — and any stored setting that
    contained one (widget configuration, theme options, many plugins’ settings)
    became unreadable and was silently lost, on a restore that reported success.
    Backups taken from this release on are correct; ones taken before it still
    carry the fault.
  • Fix: a restore could stop part-way through the database and leave the site
    half-restored.     A table whose full name was 52 to 55 characters long could
    not be swapped into place, which ended the restore with some tables replaced
    and the rest not. It mostly affected sites with a custom table prefix and
    WooCommerce installed. Such a table is now restored directly and named in the
    report, as three other cases already were.
  • Fix: asking a site to restore while it was already busy with a backup or
    restore raised a PHP fatal error instead of politely declining, so the site
    logged a critical error and your maintenance provider was told the site had
    broken rather than that it was busy.

1.29.1

  • Maintenance: coding-standard clean-up in the one-click sign-in code and
    the settings defaults. No behaviour changes.

1.29.0

  • New: one-click sign-in from your maintenance provider. Your provider can
    open this site’s admin as an administrator without a password, over the same
    signed connection it already uses to update and back up the site. Each
    sign-in uses a link that works exactly once, for one minute, for one named
    administrator, and is written to the activity log with the account it used.
    A switch on the Bulwarden screen, beside the credentials, turns it off — and
    turning it off closes the route, not only the button.

1.28.2

  • Fix: the progress of a file restore is now reported correctly when it
    finishes.     The step that writes a backup’s files back ended by reporting
    that it had written none of them — a completed restore showed
    “0 of 93,680 files, 0%” beside a count of the files it had just written.
    The two figures were also counted differently: the total included the
    backup’s database dump and its description alongside the files, so it could
    never be reached however many files were restored. It now counts the
    backup’s files, and every one of them is reported either as written or as
    deliberately left alone — this site’s own wp-config.php, Bulwarden
    itself, and WordPress’ drop-ins are never overwritten, and your hub now says
    so instead of leaving the difference unexplained.

1.28.1

  • Fix: a restore no longer spends most of its time waiting to be asked to
    carry on.     A restore runs in rounds, and at the end of each one the plugin
    asked WordPress’ scheduler to come straight back for the next — except that
    the request was made from inside the scheduler, which refuses it. So the work
    only continued when a visitor happened to arrive, or after a three-minute
    safety timer, and on a quiet site — which is most sites being restored — a
    restore took hours of waiting for minutes of work. On sites where WordPress’
    own scheduler is switched off in favour of a real cron job, which is the
    usual advice for a site that matters, nothing continued the restore at all
    between those cron runs. Each round now asks for the next one directly.

1.28.0

  • New: a banner on a site that has the plugin but is not connected to
    anyone.     Until a site is paired with a maintenance hub the plugin does
    nothing at all — no backups, no scans, nothing watched — and from the
    dashboard that is indistinguishable from a plugin quietly working. Anyone who
    can install plugins now sees a notice saying so, with the way to connect the
    site one click away, and it can be put off for a month at a time. The support
    widget on the dashboard no longer says Bulwarden maintains a site that nobody
    has agreed to maintain.
  • New: a way to ask Bulwarden for help when there is no maintenance provider
    at all.     The Request help button on the dashboard writes to whoever looks
    after the site, which is no use to somebody who installed this and has nobody.
    The plugin’s own settings screen now carries a short form that reaches
    Bulwarden directly, and says exactly what it sends: the site’s address, its
    WordPress and PHP versions and the reply address typed into it. Nothing else,
    and no keys.
  • New: the hub is told whether a backup encryption passphrase has been set —
    the fact that there is one, never the passphrase itself, which stays on this
    site and is never sent anywhere. Without one every backup stops before it
    starts, and an agency previously found that out from a failed run at three in
    the morning rather than from the setup nobody finished.
  • New: five more malware detections, from a study of 400,000 production
    webservers (Kasturi et al., Mistrust Plugins You Must): code that redefines
    a built-in PHP function instead of loading the real one, a function name
    assembled from fragments and then called, a file written to disk, made
    executable and run, code that deletes the file it ran from, and the branding
    “nulled” plugin marketplaces stamp into the paid plugins they give away with
    something added.

Earlier versions

The changelog for 1.27.3 and earlier is in changelog.txt, shipped with the plugin.

short_description: Site agent for health monitoring, malware scanning, encrypted backups and remote updates, driven by a Bulwarden hub you connect it to.
description:
Bulwarden is the site agent, installed on each managed WordPress site. It
exposes a signed REST API (jgm/v1) that a Bulwarden hub calls to read
health and security data, run checks and trigger updates. The hub is a separate
application — it is not part of this plugin — and this plugin talks to no hub
at all until you pair it with one. On its own it sends nothing anywhere.

It is built for the person who is responsible for a site they did not build:
an agency looking after forty of them, or an owner who wants one place that
answers “is this thing all right?” without logging into it.

What it reports

  • Site health — WordPress, PHP and plugin versions, pending updates, disk
    usage, and WordPress’ own Site Health tests, collected in one snapshot.
  • A full plugin and theme inventory, with each item’s version, whether it
    is active, whether an update is waiting, and whether it came from
    WordPress.org at all — which is what lets a hub match it against a CVE feed.
  • Must-use plugins, which WordPress runs on every single request with
    nothing activating them and no way to switch one off from the admin. Nothing
    else in wp-admin lists them properly, and dropping a file there is the tidiest
    way to install a backdoor.
  • Configuration-level security checks with a posture score — file editing,
    directory listing, XML-RPC, debug output, and the rest of the settings that
    quietly decide how exposed a site is.
  • Unfinished updates. An update that already replaced a site’s files can
    still fail to finish, and neither state clears itself: a pending database
    schema upgrade that every administrator is sent to and the public site hides
    completely, or a leftover .maintenance lock from an updater that died
    mid-copy. Both are reported, and both can be finished from the hub by running
    exactly what WordPress itself would have run.
  • Email delivery. WordPress keeps no record of the mail a site sends: when
    a contact form stops delivering or an order confirmation never arrives, the
    error is raised and thrown away. This counts what was attempted, what failed
    and why, and reports which transport is doing it — PHP’s mail(), an SMTP
    server, or the plugin that configured one. No part of any message is stored:
    not the recipient, not the subject, not the body.

What it finds

  • A malware scan in three layers. Every core and WordPress.org file is
    verified against its published checksums, so a modified file is found
    whether or not anybody has written a signature for what was put in it; then
    every file is read for the code patterns webshells and injected backdoors
    actually use. Findings carry the file, the line and a short excerpt.
  • Backdoors that arrive dressed as an ordinary plugin — a forged
    administrator login, a privileged action gated on a key baked into the file,
    an account created from hard-coded credentials, users hidden from the users
    list. A plugin absent from WordPress.org has no published files to check it
    against, so without this a hostile one surfaced only as unverifiable.
  • A plugin hiding itself. Malware that conceals a plugin does it by
    answering the question before WordPress can — and the hidden plugin is then
    also the one plugin whose files are never checked. The scan counts what is on
    disk itself and compares.
  • Server-configuration files. .htaccess, php.ini and .user.ini are
    the one part of a WordPress install that changes what the server does
    rather than what WordPress does, and nothing in wp-admin shows them. A file
    set to run before every request, a rule that makes uploaded images execute as
    PHP, a redirect that only fires for search engines: all reported, with the
    line. Nothing is ever changed for you — a good share of those directives are
    written deliberately by a host or a security plugin, and the point is that
    you get to decide which.
  • Leftover files. An interrupted backup, a finished restore and a migration
    plugin all leave things behind and none of them clean up: a
    wp-config.php.bak the web server hands out as plain text, a database.sql
    in the web root, an installer that overwrites the site with no login. Found,
    measured, and removable from the hub — and the site decides what may be
    deleted, so a stale list can only ever be refused.
  • Signatures that keep up. The scan’s pattern list comes from your
    provider rather than from this plugin, so a new detection reaches the site in
    hours rather than waiting for a release to travel a whole fleet. The plugin
    itself contains no malware signatures at all — a file full of them is exactly
    what a hosting provider’s own malware scanner flags — and the site keeps the
    list it receives in its database.
  • A scan that starts itself. When a plugin WordPress.org does not publish
    appears in the plugins or must-use folder, the site starts a scan within
    seconds and tells your provider what set it off, instead of waiting for the
    next scheduled one. Fake plugins are how most WordPress break-ins arrive, and
    a scan is a cheap thing to be wrong about: nothing is blocked, quarantined or
    deleted — the site looks, and your provider decides.

What it does

  • Remote core, plugin and theme updates, wrapped in maintenance mode so
    visitors never see a half-updated site — and taken off the host’s PHP time
    limit, so a core update on shared hosting finishes instead of being killed
    part-way.
  • Zero-knowledge encrypted backups. The archive is built and encrypted on
    this server    , under a passphrase that is never transmitted anywhere;
    only the ciphertext is uploaded. Nobody — including whoever runs the hub —
    can read a backup without that passphrase.
  • Restores that fail safely. The same thing in reverse, and it can put back
    the database alone if that is all that broke. Every table is rebuilt beside
    the live one and swapped in only once it is complete, so a restore stopped by
    a timeout or a server limit leaves the database exactly as it was rather than
    half-replaced — and picks itself back up where it stopped. What could not be
    done is counted and reported rather than discarded, so a restore that ran into
    trouble says so instead of reporting success.
  • Page tracing. Your provider can ask this site to render one of its own
    public pages and report which file produced each line of the HTML — core, a
    plugin, the theme, a must-use plugin. It answers the question nothing in
    WordPress answers: which plugin adds the Google Fonts tag, or the tracking
    script, or the markup nobody can find a setting for. The page is never
    altered to do it.
  • WP-Cron on a schedule that actually runs. A site with no visitors runs no
    cron, which is how scheduled posts, order emails and licence checks quietly
    stop.
  • A support card on the dashboard naming whoever maintains the site, how to
    reach them, and a Request help button that files a ticket with them
    directly — attached to the right site, without the owner having to explain
    which one.
  • An activity log on the site itself, append-only, recording everything that
    changed this site or sent part of it somewhere — and which side asked. Updates
    installed by your provider and anything that failed with them, backups,
    restores, scans, repairs, deleted leftovers, a file read off the server, a
    traced page, and every change to the credentials, the passphrase or the
    provider details. WordPress records what changed and never who asked, and the
    answer belongs on your own server rather than only in somebody else’s console.

Pairing

On activation the plugin provisions an API key + secret. Copy the connect
string from the Bulwarden entry in the WordPress admin menu and paste
it into the hub’s “Connect a site” form. Your provider’s support details are
then pushed to the site automatically by the hub and appear on the dashboard.

No hub account yet? Until the site is paired, the plugin’s banner and settings
screen offer Start a free trial, which opens the Bulwarden hub’s pricing
page (https://hub.bulwarden.net/pricing/) in a new tab. Start a trial there,
set your password from the email you receive, choose “Connect a site” in the
hub and paste the connect string. Opening that page sends nothing from this
site; it is an ordinary link.

Security

Hub → client requests are authenticated with the per-site API key and an
HMAC-SHA256 signature over the method, route, timestamp, a single-use nonce and
the body. The nonce is what makes a signature good exactly once: it is recorded
when the request arrives and refused if it comes back, so a captured request
cannot be replayed. Timestamps outside a 5-minute window are rejected outright,
which is also how long a nonce has to be remembered for. The secret never
travels on the wire — it lives only in this plugin and in the hub webapp.

Privacy

Bulwarden is a client agent: on its own it sends data nowhere. Pairing this
site with a hub (yours, or your maintenance provider’s) is an explicit,
opt-in action — you choose when to copy the connect string from the Bulwarden
screen in the WordPress admin menu and hand it to that hub. Nothing is
transmitted before that.

Once paired, data only moves in these cases:

  • Health, inventory, and security checks. The paired hub reads these from
    this site’s signed REST API when it polls or when a check is requested —
    WordPress/plugin/theme versions and update status, a full plugin & theme
    inventory, disk usage, and the configuration-level security posture score.
  • Backups, only when triggered (the Settings screen’s “Back up now”
    button, or a request from the paired hub): the full site is archived and
    encrypted on this server with a passphrase that is never transmitted
    anywhere, then the ciphertext is uploaded to the hub. Only someone who has
    the passphrase can decrypt a backup — the hub operator cannot read its
    contents.
  • Malware scan results, only when a scan is triggered (admin- or
    hub-initiated): findings (type, severity, file path, line, and a short
    excerpt) are sent to the hub that requested the scan.
  • Finishing an interrupted update, when the paired hub asks. Nothing is
    sent in that exchange; the site runs WordPress’ own database upgrade, or
    deletes an expired .maintenance lock file, and reports the outcome.
  • Server-configuration files, when the paired hub asks: the contents of
    this site’s .htaccess, php.ini and .user.ini files, so the hub can show
    what is in them and when they last changed. These are configuration, not
    content — no post, page, media file or user data is read.
  • Email counters, as part of the health snapshot: how many messages this
    site attempted and how many failed over the last seven days, the error text
    the mail server returned, and which transport is sending. No part of any
    message is recorded     — not the recipient, not the subject, not the body.
  • A traced page, only when the hub asks for one: the HTML of a single
    public page of this site, exactly as an anonymous visitor would receive it,
    plus the file paths and line numbers that produced it. No file contents are
    read and no logged-in view is ever rendered.

Independently of any hub pairing, this plugin verifies WordPress core and
wordpress.org-hosted plugin files by comparing local file hashes against the
public checksum APIs at api.wordpress.org and downloads.wordpress.org.
Those requests carry only what identifies the release to look up — the
WordPress version and locale, and each plugin’s slug and version. No file
contents, hashes, URLs or user data are sent: the reference checksums come
back and the comparison happens here, on this server.

Bulwarden does not call home on activation, does not collect analytics, and
stores data on no server this site hasn’t been explicitly connected to. The
hub itself is a separate service outside this plugin’s control; consult your
provider for how it handles the data described above.

External services

This plugin connects to the services below. Nothing here runs on activation.

Your Bulwarden hub

Bulwarden is the site-side agent for a hub — the management application an
agency or site owner runs to watch and maintain a fleet of WordPress sites. The
hub is a separate product and is not part of this plugin.

The default hosted hub is operated by Bulwarden at https://bulwarden.net/ —
terms of use: https://bulwarden.net/terms/ , privacy policy:
https://bulwarden.net/privacy/ . A hub can also be self-hosted, or run by the
maintenance provider you buy from, in which case this plugin talks to that
provider’s server instead and their terms and privacy policy apply.

No connection to any hub exists until you make one. You pair a site by
copying the connect string from the Bulwarden screen in the WordPress admin
menu and pasting it into the hub; before that the plugin contacts no hub at
all, and it never discovers or chooses one on its own. Once paired, data moves only in these cases:

  • When the hub asks for status. It reads this site’s signed REST API and
    receives WordPress/plugin/theme versions and update status, the full plugin
    and theme inventory, disk usage, the results of WordPress’ own Site Health
    tests, and the configuration-level security posture score.
  • When a backup runs (you press “Back up now”, or the hub requests one).
    The site is archived and encrypted here, with a passphrase that is never
    transmitted, and only the ciphertext is uploaded. The hub operator cannot
    read a backup’s contents without that passphrase.
  • When a malware scan runs (started by you or by the hub). The findings —
    type, severity, file path, line number and a short excerpt — are sent to the
    hub that asked for the scan.
  • When the hub pushes your provider’s support details — their name, logo,
    support address and accent colour — on connect and whenever they change
    them. Nothing is sent from the site in that exchange.

Every one of those requests is authenticated with this site’s own API key and
an HMAC-SHA256 signature; the shared secret never travels over the wire.

api.wordpress.org and downloads.wordpress.org

The malware scan verifies WordPress core and wordpress.org-hosted plugins
against their published checksums, using WordPress.org’s own public APIs at
https://api.wordpress.org/core/checksums/1.0/ and
https://downloads.wordpress.org/plugin-checksums/. This happens whenever a
scan runs, whether or not the site is paired with a hub.

These requests identify only the release being looked up: the WordPress version
and locale, and each installed plugin’s slug and version. No file contents,
hashes, site URL or user data are sent — the reference checksums are returned
and compared locally.

These are WordPress.org services, covered by the WordPress.org privacy policy:
https://wordpress.org/about/privacy/

screenshots.caption:
The Bulwarden screen at a glance: whether the site is connected, whether
backups are encrypted, when the last backup and scan ran, and how current
the scanner's signature list is.

Connecting the site: the connect string you paste into your hub, and the
API credentials behind it.

Backups: a run in progress showing the phase it has reached, its log and a
cancel button, above the encryption passphrase and the folders left out of
the archive.

The malware scan: what the last one found, grouped by kind, and how much of
the site could be checked against the files WordPress.org published.

The activity log: an append-only record of credential changes, backups,
restores, scans and repairs, including the ones the hub triggered.
The dashboard support card — who maintains this site, how to reach them, and the Request help button that files a ticket with them directly.
